items.title: Armand Hug Interview, 1976-02-13
items.q: I mean, I worked with him right towards the end. When he died, I worked right up to the time that he died. I wrote about, I guess maybe, 15, 20 tunes with him.

ctx.x: He tried to claim everybody. Yeah.

It started with him just like Jolly Roll. But if you got to know him, I mean, you know, and if he liked you. I mean, he was a funny, he was a real funny old guy. I mean, I worked with him right towards the end. When he died, I worked right up to the time that he died. I wrote about, I guess maybe, 15, 20 tunes with him. And he was wonderful to know him. I mean, the funny things that he told me, you know? Because all the Walden's musicians had funny stories.
You know, we got about eight and a half hours of Nick on tape. Did I ever tell you that? More than that.

items.title: Dominic James "Nick" La Rocca Interview, 1958-06-09
items.q: Arm and Hug being a young man, I didn't think it was the right thing for me to do to contact this boy because this program was put on by the WDSU programming department.

ctx.x: There's an answer there to this, WDSU. Alright, this is WDSU channel 6, I'm sorry, WDSU TV channel 6, New Orleans, WDSU Broadcasting Corporation, 520 Royal Street, New Orleans 16, Louisiana, Tulane 4371. January 4th, 1957, Mr. Nick LaRocca, 2218 Cousin Street, New Orleans 13, Louisiana. Dear Nick, our manager, Mr. Robert Swayze has passed to me your letter of January 13th relative to a program on jazz music which we carried in the summer of 1935. I have made a rather thorough search for the script of this program…

Almond Hug with regards with regards with what has been said. Arm and Hug being a young man, I didn't think it was the right thing for me to do to contact this boy because this program was put on by the WDSU programming department. And all this was all mapped out and planned before they went on the air what was to say. Furthermore, if you took the Dixieland Licks away from Arm and Hug, he wouldn't even play piano because that's all he plays, Dixieland Licks, to embellish his music with. There's a man probably 40…
No, I never... I don't know who this man is, but this is before my time.

items.title: Armand Hug Interview, 1965-09-13
items.q: For instance, Nick LaRocca always said this, that that when they went to New York with their band, they played a different type of jazz.

ctx.x: I think this brings to mind something else. It's kind of a confused tradition in New Orleans that's been brought up that the glorification of the older musicians by critics and by fans has often overemphasized the older Negro musicians. I think we had some rabid white musicians who'd complain about this like Nick Garaka in kind of extreme terms and it's been sort of a cluttered image that's been presented to the public. You as a person who understudied the earlier jazz musicians, colored and white, might be able…

Well, I'll put it the way Nick LaRocca put it, as you say. I think that the jazz music belongs to New Orleans. You hate to get into something where you say which was better, was the colored music better or the white jazz music better? I think that stuff stuff

music had its place where they had the marching bands, which was a definite, a particular style of New Orleans, which I think belonged entirely, mostly, to the to the to the colored people. However, I do believe this, that the white musicians brought jazz to a higher level, to a higher standard, in when they brought it to New York. For instance, Nick LaRocca always said this, that that when they went to New York with their band, they played a different type of jazz. In fact, if you listen to it, if you listen to…
